title: Anthropic ships Claude Dashboards and Claude Motion in beta
subtitle: Dashboards queries data warehouses in plain English and renders live charts; Motion turns prompts into animated explainers by writing code — not by generating video frames.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic has pushed two new tools into beta inside Claude: Claude Dashboards, which builds live, queryable dashboards from plain-language questions against company data, and Claude Motion, which generates short animated explainers from a prompt. Dashboards connects to Snowflake, Databricks, Amazon Redshift, ClickHouse, BigQuery, and Salesforce, and can export to external BI tools. Motion is scoped to Team and Enterprise plans only. Both features ship off by default and must be enabled by an organization admin. Alongside the beta launches, Claude Docs, Slides, and Design have exited beta and are now generally available on every plan — including Free. The standalone claude.design website will close on December 14, 2026.

The design decision that distinguishes Motion from the current crop of AI video tools is that it does not call a video generation model. Instead, it writes code that animates text, charts, shapes, and existing images in the user's own work — the way a motion designer would key frames in After Effects, not the way Sora or Veo invent pixels from a prompt. That means no hallucinated faces, no fabricated footage, and much tighter control over what appears on screen. Runway, named as a launch partner, says any Motion output can be exported into its editor for further work; Adobe and HeyGen handoffs are also supported.

This is the second time in six months Anthropic has shipped a horizontal office-productivity surface — Docs, Slides, Design, now Dashboards and Motion — rather than a new frontier model. The strategic read is that Claude's growth story is pivoting away from "the smartest chatbot" and toward being the application layer that competes with Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Workspace agents on the merits of outputs people actually paste into decks and board meetings. The free-tier Docs/Slides/Design GA puts that competition in front of a much wider audience in a single move.

For learners, the useful observation is architectural: Motion solves video explainers by writing deterministic animation code, not by letting a diffusion model guess. When the output needs to be factually faithful — a company's quarterly numbers, a legal workflow, a safety-critical diagram — generating code that runs over your data is almost always safer than generating pixels. Watching how Dashboards translates a plain-English question into a SQL plan, and how Motion compiles a prompt into an animation script, is the clearest demonstration yet of why the "LLM as a code-writer" pattern keeps winning over end-to-end generative pipelines.
